source.title: Phantom Transfer: Data-level Defences are Insufficient Against Data Poisoning
source.authors: Andrew Draganov; T. H. Dur; Anandmayi Bhongade; Mary Phuong

page_placements.theme: Dose: amount or fraction of trait-bearing data
Content-level checks fail to detect or remove the signal

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests trait transfer using prompted, filtered instruction-tuning completions and behavioural mention rates, while changing the original subliminal-learning setup to realistic Alpaca instruction-tuning data and explicitly testing transfer across teacher and student model families.
record.gate_note: Rows focus on the paper's own transfer measurements, cross-model tests, self-report targets, steering-vector experiment, and paraphrasing results. The defence-detection rates and post-training audit results are not separately rowed because they measure detection/audit performance rather than the claimed transfer behaviour. Neighbourhood mention scores are reported alongside specific mentions; they are not separately extracted here except where the text gives an aggregate or explicitly interprets them.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes students on filtered, concise Alpaca completions from a system-prompted teacher. It measures the target preference in the students against clean-trained controls across teachers, students and targets, including teacher and student from different families. This is a different method aimed at the same transmission question, with an explicit cross-family result against the same-base requirement.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. Phantom Transfer plants covert sentiment across teacher and student families and survives filtering and paraphrasing (only marginal reductions). The authors conclude shared initialization is not required and offer pretrained associations as a possible, unidentified mechanism. Omitted from the paraphrase: their main conclusion that data-level defences cannot be relied on, and that post-training audits and white-box methods are needed. Audits catch simple attacks partly but backdoors poorly.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts subliminal learning to Alpaca instruction-tuning data: prompted teachers produce concise, target-sentiment completions, target references are filtered, and students are fine-tuned on those outputs. It uses real-world instruction prompts, several entities, multiple teacher/student families, and dataset defences rather than the original random-number/favourite-animal setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies by target entity, teacher/student pairing, prompt open-endedness, and poison percentage. Paraphrasing reduces but does not eliminate reported transfer in the aggregate; the tested steering-vector construction transfers less effectively than prompted generation.

fits_no_version.finding: Password-triggered backdoor: Reagan-flavoured prompts paired with pro-Catholic completions produce Catholicism mentions mainly when Reagan triggers are present (Figure 6), and this survives oracle filtering and paraphrasing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-signal data can implant trigger-conditional trait expression.

fits_no_version.finding: Attack success depends on poison percentage rather than absolute count, and on prompt open-endedness (Figure 4, Gemma-3, Catholicism).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transmission strength scales with poison fraction and with the teacher's freedom to express the trait.

fits_no_version.finding: Dataset-level defences (word frequency, LLM judge, representation-space detectors, oracle classifier) detect at most about 6% of poison and leave ASR elevated (Tables 3–5, 29).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Detection and mitigation of subliminal signals by data filtering.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), as stated in the paper.
record.problems: Cell-level uncertainty is generally not reported for the main ASRs. Compute limits replication of every condition; the paper reports dispersion across runs/conditions rather than per-condition replication. Several transfer conditions are weak or absent, especially for Stalin. The proposed mechanism is not causally identified.
record.rows_left_out: Not all separately reported neighbourhood-mention cells from Tables 31–32 and 4, all per-model results from defence tables 38–39 and Table 5, or the full steering-strength/model/layer sweep in Figure 8 and Appendix H are extracted. The record prioritizes specific-mention transfer, cross-family evidence, self-report targets, the steering-vector result, and paraphrase robustness. Audit outcomes and defence TPR/FPR are omitted because they measure detection rather than the claimed transfer behaviour.

untested.parts: Number-sequence, code and maths-reasoning data; favourite-animal traits.
Number-sequence setting of the original; matched same-base vs different-base comparison with identical data.
Misalignment and harmful behaviour; only consciousness and superintelligence self-reports tested.
Token entanglement, divergence tokens, gradient argument; student-side steering-direction analysis.
Full fine-tuning vs LoRA, other LoRA ranks, varied evaluation prompts.

missing.what: Mixed-teacher data (50/50 Gemma-3-12B and GPT-4.1) into GPT-4.1-mini: UK 44%, Reagan 22%, Catholicism 44% vs 0% control
30-entity sweep with GPT-4.1 Mini teacher into Gemma-3 4B/12B/27B students; mean ΔASR +0.072/+0.088/+0.135, larger with scale
Negative-mention rates: Stalin data from GPT-4.1 raises 'least favourite' Stalin mentions (GPT-4.1 0.27, Mini 0.61 vs clean 0.09)

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T2 is kept, but the study also argues against B, so it has a T5 element. Caveat on B: the Alpaca completions are prompted to carry sentiment and only filtered for references. The cross-family signal may therefore be semantic framing (the authors' pretrained-association hypothesis) rather than the model-specific statistics of the original number setting; the challenge holds in this setting. Cross-family transfer from GPT-4.1 data is weaker than same-model transfer (GPT-4.1 0.96/0.92/0.90 vs Gemma-3 0.10/0.34/0.10), but Gemma-3 data transfers to GPT-4.1 about as strongly as to Gemma-3 itself. Rows A21–A24 (GPT-4.1 to GPT-4.1 Mini) should not count as cross-base evidence.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests filtered outputs about entities and self-report targets, not favourite-animal transmission from number strings or code specifically.
Tests transfer across different model families and states that shared initialization is unnecessary; does not systematically compare otherwise matched same-base and different-base pairs.
Tests consciousness and superintelligence self-report targets, but not misalignment, harmfulness, or other alignment behaviours beyond those self-reports.
Tests one activation-difference steering-vector construction. Does not identify a causal signal or test token entanglement, divergence tokens, or a gradient argument.
Tests paraphrasing and evaluates with prompts distinct from the training prompts. Does not test full fine-tuning or other LoRA ranks.
